```python name=sql/sql_complete.py
# ============================================================
# SQL — Structured Query Language (Every Python Dev MUST Know)
# ============================================================
# This covers everything asked in Python developer interviews

SQL_EXAMPLES = """

-- ============================================================
-- DDL — Data Definition Language (CREATE, ALTER, DROP)
-- ============================================================

CREATE TABLE users (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,           -- Auto-increment (PostgreSQL)
    name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email       VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    age         INTEGER CHECK (age >= 18),
    salary      DECIMAL(10, 2) DEFAULT 0.00,
    role        VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'user',
    is_active   BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,
    created_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at  TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    department_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(id) ON DELETE SET NULL
);

CREATE TABLE departments (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    budget      DECIMAL(15, 2)
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    product     VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    amount      DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    quantity    INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
    status      VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'pending',
    order_date  DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

-- Indexes (speed up queries)
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_date ON orders(order_date);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email_unique ON users(email);

-- Composite index
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status ON orders(user_id, status);

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(20);
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN phone;
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN name TYPE VARCHAR(200);
ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp_table;
TRUNCATE TABLE logs;  -- Delete all rows, reset auto-increment

-- ============================================================
-- DML — Data Manipulation Language (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
-- ============================================================

-- INSERT
INSERT INTO users (name, email, age, salary, role, department_id)
VALUES ('Veerababu', 'veera@test.com', 30, 75000.00, 'admin', 1);

-- Insert multiple rows
INSERT INTO users (name, email, age, salary, department_id) VALUES
    ('Alice', 'alice@test.com', 25, 60000.00, 1),
    ('Bob', 'bob@test.com', 35, 80000.00, 2),
    ('Charlie', 'charlie@test.com', 28, 55000.00, 1),
    ('Diana', 'diana@test.com', 32, 90000.00, 3);

-- INSERT from SELECT (copy data)
INSERT INTO archived_users (name, email)
SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE is_active = FALSE;

-- UPSERT (Insert or Update on conflict)
INSERT INTO users (email, name, salary)
VALUES ('veera@test.com', 'Veera Updated', 80000)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET
    name = EXCLUDED.name,
    salary = EXCLUDED.salary,
    updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;

-- UPDATE
UPDATE users SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE department_id = 1;
UPDATE users SET is_active = FALSE WHERE last_login < '2025-01-01';

-- UPDATE with JOIN
UPDATE orders o
SET status = 'cancelled'
FROM users u
WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND u.is_active = FALSE;

-- DELETE
DELETE FROM users WHERE is_active = FALSE AND created_at < '2024-01-01';

-- DELETE with subquery
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE user_id IN (SELECT id FROM users WHERE is_active = FALSE);

-- ============================================================
-- SELECT — Querying Data (MOST IMPORTANT!)
-- ============================================================

-- Basic SELECT
SELECT * FROM users;
SELECT name, email, salary FROM users;
SELECT DISTINCT role FROM users;
SELECT name AS full_name, salary AS monthly_pay FROM users;

-- WHERE clause with operators
SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 25;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE role = 'admin' AND is_active = TRUE;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE role IN ('admin', 'moderator');
SELECT * FROM users WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 100000;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'V%';          -- Starts with V
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE '%kumar%';      -- Contains kumar
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name ILIKE '%veera%';     -- Case-insensitive (PostgreSQL)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email IS NOT NULL;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE department_id IS NULL;
SELECT * FROM users WHERE NOT (age < 25 OR salary < 50000);

-- ORDER BY
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY salary DESC;
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY department_id ASC, salary DESC;
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY created_at DESC NULLS LAST;

-- LIMIT & OFFSET (Pagination)
SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;  -- Page 3, 10 per page

-- ============================================================
-- AGGREGATE FUNCTIONS
-- ============================================================
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users;                                -- Total rows
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department_id) FROM users;           -- Unique departments
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM users;                             -- Total salary
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM users;                             -- Average salary
SELECT MIN(salary), MAX(salary) FROM users;                -- Min and Max
SELECT ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary FROM users;    -- Rounded

-- ============================================================
-- GROUP BY + HAVING
-- ============================================================
-- GROUP BY: Group rows that have the same values
-- HAVING: Filter groups (WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups)

-- Count users per department
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM users
GROUP BY department_id;

-- Average salary per role
SELECT role, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary, COUNT(*) AS count
FROM users
GROUP BY role
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

-- Departments with more than 5 users
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM users
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

-- Total order amount per user, only users with > $1000 total
SELECT user_id, SUM(amount * quantity) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING SUM(amount * quantity) > 1000
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

-- ============================================================
-- JOINS — Combining Tables (CRITICAL INTERVIEW TOPIC!)
-- ============================================================

-- INNER JOIN — Only matching rows from BOTH tables
SELECT u.name, u.email, d.name AS department
FROM users u
INNER JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id;

-- LEFT JOIN — ALL rows from left table + matching from right
-- Non-matching right side = NULL
SELECT u.name, d.name AS department
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id;
-- Includes users WITH NO department (department = NULL)

-- RIGHT JOIN — ALL rows from right table + matching from left
SELECT u.name, d.name AS department
FROM users u
RIGHT JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id;
-- Includes departments WITH NO users

-- FULL OUTER JOIN — ALL rows from BOTH tables
SELECT u.name, d.name AS department
FROM users u
FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id;

-- CROSS JOIN — Cartesian product (every combination)
SELECT u.name, d.name
FROM users u
CROSS JOIN departments d;

-- SELF JOIN — Join table with itself
-- Find users in same department
SELECT a.name AS user1, b.name AS user2, a.department_id
FROM users a
JOIN users b ON a.department_id = b.department_id AND a.id < b.id;

-- Multiple JOINs
SELECT u.name, d.name AS department, o.product, o.amount
FROM users u
JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
ORDER BY o.amount DESC;

-- LEFT JOIN to find users with NO orders
SELECT u.name, u.email
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- ============================================================
-- SUBQUERIES
-- ============================================================

-- Subquery in WHERE
SELECT name, salary
FROM users
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM users);

-- Subquery in FROM (Derived table)
SELECT dept_stats.department, dept_stats.avg_salary
FROM (
    SELECT department_id AS department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
    FROM users
    GROUP BY department_id
) dept_stats
WHERE dept_stats.avg_salary > 60000;

-- EXISTS (check if subquery returns any rows)
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o
    WHERE o.user_id = u.id AND o.amount > 500
);

-- NOT EXISTS (users who never ordered)
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id
);

-- IN with subquery
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE department_id IN (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE budget > 100000
);

-- Correlated subquery (references outer query)
SELECT u.name, u.salary,
    (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM users u2
     WHERE u2.department_id = u.department_id) AS dept_avg
FROM users u;

-- ============================================================
-- WINDOW FUNCTIONS (Advanced — Very Common in Interviews!)
-- ============================================================
-- Perform calculations across a SET of rows RELATED to current row
-- Unlike GROUP BY, window functions DON'T collapse rows

-- ROW_NUMBER — Unique sequential number
SELECT name, salary, department_id,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank
FROM users;

-- RANK — Same rank for ties, gaps after ties
-- DENSE_RANK — Same rank for ties, NO gaps
SELECT name, salary,
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM users;

-- PARTITION BY — Window per group
-- Rank within each department
SELECT name, salary, department_id,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM users;

-- Top 3 highest paid per department
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT name, salary, department_id,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM users
) ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

-- Running total
SELECT order_date, amount,
    SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM orders;

-- Moving average (last 3 orders)
SELECT order_date, amount,
    AVG(amount) OVER (
        ORDER BY order_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS moving_avg
FROM orders;

-- LAG / LEAD — Access previous/next row
SELECT name, salary,
    LAG(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS prev_salary,
    LEAD(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS next_salary,
    salary - LAG(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS salary_diff
FROM users;

-- FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE
SELECT name, salary, department_id,
    FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (
        PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC
    ) AS highest_paid_in_dept
FROM users;

-- NTILE — Divide rows into N buckets
SELECT name, salary,
    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS quartile
FROM users;

-- Percentage of total
SELECT name, salary,
    ROUND(salary * 100.0 / SUM(salary) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_total
FROM users;

-- ============================================================
-- CTE — Common Table Expressions (WITH clause)
-- ============================================================
-- Readable alternative to subqueries

WITH active_users AS (
    SELECT * FROM users WHERE is_active = TRUE
),
high_earners AS (
    SELECT * FROM active_users WHERE salary > 70000
)
SELECT h.name, h.salary, d.name AS department
FROM high_earners h
JOIN departments d ON h.department_id = d.id;

-- Recursive CTE (for hierarchical data: org charts, categories)
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    -- Base case: top-level managers
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS level
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Recursive case: employees under managers
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.level + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT * FROM org_chart ORDER BY level, name;

-- ============================================================
-- STRING FUNCTIONS
-- ============================================================
SELECT UPPER(name), LOWER(email) FROM users;
SELECT LENGTH(name), TRIM('  hello  ') FROM users;
SELECT CONCAT(name, ' - ', role) AS display FROM users;
SELECT SUBSTRING(email FROM 1 FOR 5) FROM users;  -- First 5 chars
SELECT REPLACE(email, '@test.com', '@company.com') FROM users;
SELECT SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2) AS domain FROM users;  -- PostgreSQL
SELECT COALESCE(phone, 'N/A') FROM users;  -- First non-null value

-- ============================================================
-- DATE FUNCTIONS
-- ============================================================
SELECT CURRENT_DATE, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, NOW();
SELECT DATE_PART('year', created_at) FROM users;           -- Extract year
SELECT AGE(CURRENT_DATE, created_at) FROM users;           -- Time difference
SELECT created_at + INTERVAL '30 days' FROM users;         -- Add 30 days
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month FROM orders;

-- Orders per month
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(amount) AS total_revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

-- ============================================================
-- CASE WHEN — Conditional Logic in SQL
-- ============================================================
SELECT name, salary,
    CASE
        WHEN salary >= 90000 THEN 'Senior'
        WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'Mid'
        WHEN salary >= 30000 THEN 'Junior'
        ELSE 'Intern'
    END AS level
FROM users;

-- Pivot-like aggregation
SELECT department_id,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN role = 'admin' THEN 1 END) AS admin_count,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN role = 'user' THEN 1 END) AS user_count,
    SUM(CASE WHEN is_active THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS active_salary
FROM users
GROUP BY department_id;

-- ============================================================
-- TRANSACTIONS
-- ============================================================
BEGIN;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;

-- If anything fails, ROLLBACK; else COMMIT;
COMMIT;

-- SAVEPOINT (partial rollback)
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT sp1;
INSERT INTO logs VALUES ('step 1');
SAVEPOINT sp2;
INSERT INTO logs VALUES ('step 2');  -- This fails
ROLLBACK TO sp2;                     -- Undo only step 2
COMMIT;                              -- Step 1 is committed

-- ============================================================
-- VIEWS
-- ============================================================
CREATE VIEW active_user_summary AS
SELECT u.name, u.email, d.name AS department, u.salary
FROM users u
JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id
WHERE u.is_active = TRUE;

-- Use like a table
SELECT * FROM active_user_summary WHERE salary > 60000;

-- Materialized view (cached, for performance)
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY month;

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue;  -- Manually refresh

-- ============================================================
-- EXPLAIN — Query Optimization
-- ============================================================
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id)
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.name;
-- Shows: Seq Scan, Index Scan, Hash Join, Sort, cost, actual time

""";
```

```python name=sql/sqlalchemy_complete.py
# ============================================================
# SQLAlchemy — Python ORM for SQL Databases
# ============================================================
from sqlalchemy import (
    create_engine, Column, Integer, String, Float, Boolean,
    DateTime, ForeignKey, Text, Index, UniqueConstraint,
    select, func, and_, or_, desc, asc, text, update, delete
)
from sqlalchemy.orm import (
    DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship,
    Session, sessionmaker, joinedload, selectinload
)
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional

# ============================================================
# MODEL DEFINITION (SQLAlchemy 2.0 style)
# ============================================================
class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class Department(Base):
    __tablename__ = "departments"
    
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), unique=True)
    budget: Mapped[Optional[float]] = mapped_column(Float, default=0)
    
    # Relationship
    users: Mapped[list["User"]] = relationship(back_populates="department")
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Department(id={self.id}, name={self.name})"

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    __table_args__ = (
        Index("idx_user_email", "email"),
        UniqueConstraint("email", name="uq_user_email"),
    )
    
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100))
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(255), unique=True)
    salary: Mapped[float] = mapped_column(Float, default=0)
    is_active: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(Boolean, default=True)
    department_id: Mapped[Optional[int]] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("departments.id"))
    created_at: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(DateTime, default=datetime.now)
    
    # Relationships
    department: Mapped[Optional["Department"]] = relationship(back_populates="users")
    orders: Mapped[list["Order"]] = relationship(back_populates="user", cascade="all, delete-orphan")

class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))
    product: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(200))
    amount: Mapped[float] = mapped_column(Float)
    status: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(20), default="pending")
    
    user: Mapped["User"] = relationship(back_populates="orders")

# ============================================================
# DATABASE CONNECTION
# ============================================================
engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///app.db",      # or "postgresql://user:pass@localhost/dbname"
    echo=True,                # Log SQL statements
    pool_size=5,              # Connection pool
    max_overflow=10,
)
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine)

# ============================================================
# CRUD OPERATIONS
# ============================================================

# --- CREATE ---
with SessionLocal() as session:
    dept = Department(name="Engineering", budget=500000)
    session.add(dept)
    session.flush()  # Get dept.id without committing
    
    user = User(name="Veera", email="veera@test.com", salary=75000, department=dept)
    session.add(user)
    
    # Bulk insert
    session.add_all([
        User(name="Alice", email="alice@test.com", salary=60000, department=dept),
        User(name="Bob", email="bob@test.com", salary=80000),
    ])
    session.commit()

# --- READ ---
with SessionLocal() as session:
    # Get by primary key
    user = session.get(User, 1)
    
    # Query with filters
    stmt = select(User).where(
        and_(
            User.is_active == True,
            User.salary > 50000,
        )
    ).order_by(desc(User.salary)).limit(10)
    
    users = session.scalars(stmt).all()
    
    # Eager loading (avoid N+1 problem!)
    stmt = select(User).options(
        joinedload(User.department),     # JOIN in same query
        selectinload(User.orders),       # Separate SELECT IN query
    )
    users_with_relations = session.scalars(stmt).unique().all()
    
    # Aggregation
    stmt = select(
        User.department_id,
        func.count(User.id).label("user_count"),
        func.avg(User.salary).label("avg_salary"),
    ).group_by(User.department_id).having(func.count(User.id) > 1)
    
    results = session.execute(stmt).all()

# --- UPDATE ---
with SessionLocal() as session:
    # Single update
    user = session.get(User, 1)
    user.salary = 80000
    session.commit()
    
    # Bulk update
    stmt = update(User).where(User.department_id == 1).values(salary=User.salary * 1.1)
    session.execute(stmt)
    session.commit()

# --- DELETE ---
with SessionLocal() as session:
    user = session.get(User, 1)
    session.delete(user)
    session.commit()
    
    # Bulk delete
    stmt = delete(User).where(User.is_active == False)
    session.execute(stmt)
    session.commit()

# ============================================================
# ASYNC SQLAlchemy (for FastAPI)
# ============================================================
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, AsyncSession, async_sessionmaker

async_engine = create_async_engine("postgresql+asyncpg://user:pass@localhost/db")
AsyncSessionLocal = async_sessionmaker(async_engine, class_=AsyncSession)

async def get_users():
    async with AsyncSessionLocal() as session:
        stmt = select(User).where(User.is_active == True)
        result = await session.scalars(stmt)
        return result.all()
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: Functions that perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row, WITHOUT collapsing rows (unlike GROUP BY).
Indexes speed up SELECT queries by creating a B-tree (or hash) data structure.
Common Table Expression (WITH clause). A named temporary result set.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.
quiz.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. You can't use aggregate functions in WHERE.
